title:
Secure Embedded
Water Tank Controller
lines: Finley Burns
CYCS 3240 Design Presentation
November 17, 2026
notes: I designed a C17 controller for one simulated water tank. I will explain the control rule, the sensor and serial interfaces, and how I test them. The implementation has progressed since the preliminary design. I will separate the design choices from the results that now verify them.

title: Project scope
lines: One tank, one level sensor, and one inlet valve
C17 on an emulated STM32F4 Cortex-M4
Serial commands for the operating thresholds
Host tools for x86-64 and ARM64 on all three operating systems
notes: I kept the scope small so the control behavior and security checks are manageable. The tank is simulated, so I do not need a physical board or plumbing. I originally proposed Rust, but switched to C because the course requires C or C++. Renode still supplies the emulated processor and peripherals. The serial interface is enough for this project, so I am not adding networking or a dashboard. Source: comprehensive design, project scope; https://renode.readthedocs.io/en/latest/introduction/testing.html The native host tools support x86-64 and ARM64 on Windows, macOS and Linux. Cortex-M4 is the separate embedded ARM target. All six host CI jobs now pass.

title: Valve decisions
lines: Below 30%: open the inlet
Above 70%: close the inlet
At either threshold or between them: keep the previous state
Invalid input: close the inlet and report a fault
notes: The controller uses hysteresis. Two thresholds give the valve a clear operating range instead of making it switch around one target. The exact endpoints matter: at 30 or 70 percent, the previous state stays in place. The tests check both an initially open and initially closed valve. When valid sensor input returns after a fault, the usual rule resumes. If the reading is between the thresholds, the valve remains closed because the fault closed it. Source: Source/src/controller.c and file-driven control tests.

title: The control loop
lines: Sample the level every 100 ms of simulated time
Check the value, validity flag, and sample age
Calculate the valve state with the shared control function
Service bounded serial input, then write PD12
notes: The control decision runs every 100 milliseconds. A sensor sample older than 300 milliseconds is invalid. A sequence number protects the RAM sensor record against a partial update, and the level is checked before conversion. The firmware calculates the control decision before bounded serial service, then writes the GPIO when that service returns. This differs slightly from the original immediate-GPIO pseudocode. The measured load tests kept the virtual schedule. Source: final report, firmware and ARM sensor/serial evidence.

title: Command checks
lines: HMAC-SHA256 checks the command contents
Both thresholds change only after every check passes
Rejected commands leave the existing settings alone
No encryption or replay protection in this scope
notes: The command contains two thresholds and an HMAC-SHA256 tag. Mbed TLS 3.6.7 verifies the tag. Format, conversion and range checks still apply, and both settings change together only after the complete command passes. The next control tick uses the new settings. Replay is accepted because the design has no nonce or counter, and HMAC does not encrypt traffic. Five HMAC checks and invalid-command cases passed. Sources: final report; Mbed TLS 3.6.7 release; RFC 4231.

title: Keeping control running
lines: Bound the receive queue and command length
Limit serial work to 32 bytes and one tag check per cycle
Discard malformed input and expire partial commands
Measure whether heavy input delays the control step
notes: The queue holds 256 bytes and the line buffer allows 128 bytes before LF. The loop processes at most 32 bytes and one completed line per tick. Oversized input is discarded through LF; a partial line expires above 500 milliseconds. The timer and IRQ handling are implemented. Three 60-second Renode load modes, including a 1000-byte-per-second malformed flood, recorded no missed deadlines. The injected sensor fault closed the GPIO on its checked tick. This establishes virtual timing, not physical timing. Source: Evidence/ARM_Sensor_Serial.

title: Tests completed
lines: 69 control cases and 18 stateful sequence steps
36 runtime scenarios and 5 HMAC checks
Windows, macOS and Linux: x86-64 and ARM64 passed
ARM sensor, serial and tank feedback tests passed
notes: The baseline also includes 23 parser files and three invocation-error checks. The runtime suite covers invalid input, age, overflow, timeout, replay and repeated authentication. I checked the actual compiler target triples in CI to establish native x86-64 and ARM64 execution. The Cortex-M4 firmware separately ran 1815 sensor/serial observations and a 600-second closed-loop model test in Renode. Sources: final report Evidence directories; GitHub Actions run 42890613662.

title: System tests
lines: Normal filling and draining, then changes in demand
Old or invalid sensor readings and recovery
Modified commands, invalid values, and replay behavior
Long runs, slow sampling, and heavy serial input
notes: The C model holds 100 litres and starts at 50, with two litres per second entering through an open inlet and one leaving under normal demand. Eighteen native runs cover changing demand, shortage, a stuck-open valve, one hour of operation, and three sampling periods. The normal native and ARM feedback runs both measured 29.9 to 70.1 percent. The full abnormal-flow and sampling matrix ran natively, while Renode tested one normal closed-loop case plus sensor and serial-load cases. Source: final report and tank evidence.

title: December submission
lines: The IEEE report explains the design and measured behavior
Source and test inputs support repeatable runs
Raw results distinguish host tests from ARM execution
The final presentation includes the results and limits
notes: The report and supporting files are prepared, and the final package passed a fresh extraction check. I have kept the November documents as design milestones and the later implementation in its own directory. The main remaining limits are physical hardware, ADC behavior, protected key storage, encryption and replay prevention. They are outside the current implementation. I can answer questions about the interfaces, threshold rule or testing choices. Source: final report and USER_GUIDE.txt.
